newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Afghan opposition insists Pakistan backs Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Afghan opposition insists Pakistan backs Taleban.

text.p: An Afghan opposition leader was quoted on Friday as saying it was the "national duty" of anti-Taleban forces attacking Kabul to capture the city because the purist Islamic militia had Pakistanis fighting at its side.
Former Afghan foreign minister Abdulrahman Ghafurzai said in an interview with a Swiss newspaper that the Taleban was getting "all sorts of aid as well as light and heavy weaponry" from Pakistan.

Ghafurzai, who said he had been named foreign minister in a provisional government just set up by all anti-Taleban forces, asserted that two weeks ago the opposition had displayed 400 Pakistanis it had captured fighting with the militia.
"These fighters have been trained in Pakistan by Pakistani officers. In these circumstances, the liberation of Kabul is a national duty," he told the Tribune de Geneve in Paris.
Pakistan, on whose territory the Taleban movement sprang up in Afghan refugee camps in the early 1990s, has frequently denied providing any military support to the militia.
Former Pakistani prime minister Benazir Bhutto, during whose rule the movement swept through Afghanistan, told Reuters Television in Colombo that her country had little to do with the Taleban.

"I think Pakistan has kept its hands off Afghanistan, but I cannot say that for others," she said, adding that the civil war suited different powers who wanted to ensure oil and gas from Central Asia did not pass through Afghanistan to Pakistan.
Opposition forces led by former defence minister Ahmed Shah Masood have moved to within 20 km north of Kabul in recent days, according to travellers arriving in the capital.
A Reuter correspondent in the city reported that the front lines were quiet after four days of heavy fighting.
Ghafurzai said the opposition wanted to Kabul to be demilitarised and was aiming to set up a national parliament, or Loya Jerga, under the auspices of the United Nations.
"This would approve a new constitution and appoint a new president. We also want to organise free nationwide elections under the supervision of the international community," he said.
"We still want to make Kabul a demilitarised zone, but for that it is necessary for the Taleban to evacuate the city so that peace negotiations can begin.
"If they agree to pull out of the city, we are ready to begin peace talks immediately. But until now, they are refusing."
